title: Atoms, Molecules and Chemical Laws
scope_note: Class IX chemistry foundations with explicit distinction of laws and chemical models
introduction: Atomic language becomes useful only when we can track what a chemical reaction preserves. We follow the reasoning from conservation through pure compounds, symbols, molecular versus ionic entities, correct formula writing and quantitative masses. Formulae are scientific representations, not arbitrary strings.

subtopics.title: Conservation of mass
subtopics.entry_question: When a candle burns in a closed vessel, why doesn't the mass simply vanish as the wax disappears?
core1a_paragraphs: The law of conservation of mass states that the total mass of a closed system is unchanged during ordinary chemical reactions, within the accuracy of the measurement. Atoms are reorganised into new substances; they are not created or destroyed in those reactions.

Open vessels can give misleading readings because gases move across the measurement boundary. Burning wax consumes oxygen from the air and produces gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour; the mass of those products must be counted.

Chemical equations use coefficients to conserve each element. This is stricter and more informative than checking only the total mass numerically, because equal masses of different elements would not establish a correctly balanced reaction.
subtopics.representation: Put reaction vessel and surrounding gas inside a dashed system boundary. Draw arrows for gas crossing only when the container is open. Use colour-coded elemental atom counts on both sides.

worked_example.problem: A sealed reaction begins with 12 g carbon and 32 g oxygen and produces only carbon dioxide. Find product mass.
steps: System is closed; no matter enters or leaves.
Initial total mass = 12 g + 32 g = 44 g.
All reactants are converted into the stated sole product.
Final CO₂ mass is 44 g.
worked_example.check: C + O₂ → CO₂ balances one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.

misconception.wrong: The mass after a reaction equals the mass of the solid products only.
misconception.why: Gases may be products and must be included in the entire closed system.
misconception.repair: Include every phase in the same weighed system.

demands.title: Follow products across physical states
demands.core1a_explanation: A mass law applies to a chosen system boundary, including gases, liquids and solids, while products can have different appearances.
demands.worked_reasoning: Burning 12 g carbon with 32 g oxygen in a sealed reaction produces 44 g CO₂ with the same atoms.

subtopics.title: Constant composition and Dalton theory
subtopics.entry_question: Why is pure water described by H₂O whether collected from rain, a river or a laboratory?
core1a_paragraphs: A pure chemical compound has a characteristic ratio of constituents. For water this ratio follows the H₂O formula: two H atoms per O atom in each molecule, implying a fixed hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio under standard isotope approximations.
Dalton's atomic ideas offered a model for fixed whole-number combinations of atoms. The historical theory was not complete: isotopes show that atoms of an element need not all have the same mass.

A sample described as 'water' may contain dissolved salts or gases, but those impurities change the mixture composition, not the composition of pure water molecules. We must distinguish compound purity from the water source.
subtopics.representation: Compare H₂O molecular diagrams from two samples; add free salt ions in one sample to show impurities without altering H₂O connectivity.

worked_example.problem: Show the mass ratio of H to O in pure H₂O using approximate atomic masses 1 and 16.
steps: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Hydrogen contribution ≈ 2 × 1 = 2; oxygen contribution ≈ 16.
Ratio 2:16 simplifies to 1:8.
worked_example.result: Hydrogen : oxygen mass ratio is approximately 1:8.
worked_example.check: This is not 2:1 by mass; the 2:1 ratio counts atoms.

misconception.wrong: The two hydrogen atoms mean water contains twice the mass of hydrogen as oxygen.
misconception.why: Atomic counts must be weighted by atomic masses.
misconception.repair: Explicitly state whether a ratio counts atoms or mass.

demands.title: Fixed ratio despite diverse sources
demands.core1a_explanation: Compound identity persists even when its surrounding mixture varies; impurities are separate components.
demands.worked_reasoning: Rainwater and seawater each contain H₂O molecules; the salts in seawater do not convert pure H₂O into a different molecule.

core1b.model_response: Isotopes of the same element have equal proton count but different neutron numbers and masses. Therefore identical mass is not universal; same elemental identity is determined by proton number.

subtopics.title: Atoms, molecules, ions and formula units
subtopics.entry_question: Is the NaCl symbol a single 'molecule' like H₂O, or does it refer to a different structural arrangement?
core1a_paragraphs: An atom is a particle of an element. A molecule is a discrete bonded group of atoms. An ion is charged because it has gained or lost electrons relative to its neutral atom or group. A formula unit gives the simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound.

Water consists of discrete H₂O molecules under ordinary conditions. Sodium chloride forms a lattice containing many Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; NaCl denotes its simplest ratio, not usually one independent NaCl molecule in the crystalline solid.

These distinctions matter when counting particles or calculating mole quantities. A mole of NaCl formula units does not mean a mole of individual two-atom salt molecules in solid salt; the counting unit is explicitly a formula unit.
subtopics.representation: Sketch one H₂O molecule with O–H edges next to a repeated lattice of Na+ and Cl- nodes. Label the unit being counted in each case.

worked_example.problem: Classify H₂O, O₂, Na⁺ and solid NaCl in elementary particle language.
steps: H₂O consists of discrete compound molecules.
O₂ consists of diatomic molecules of one element.
Na⁺ is a monatomic cation.
Solid NaCl is an ionic lattice expressed by formula units.
worked_example.result: Molecule; elemental molecule; ion; ionic formula-unit lattice.
worked_example.check: Do not equate a molecular formula and ionic lattice formula.

misconception.wrong: All formulas with two element symbols describe a two-atom molecule.
misconception.why: Ionic formulas often give the smallest whole-number ionic ratio.
misconception.repair: Identify the bonding and structural state before assigning a particle type.

demands.title: Formula unit versus molecule
demands.core1a_explanation: Different bonding structures require different counting language.
demands.worked_reasoning: NaCl(s) contains a lattice; NaCl(aq) contains solvated ions, while H₂O is molecular.

subtopics.title: Valency and charge in chemical formulae
subtopics.entry_question: Why is magnesium chloride written MgCl₂ rather than Mg₂Cl?
core1a_paragraphs: Valency summarises combining capacity in simple compounds; for ionic compounds, ion charge gives a direct constraint. Magnesium often forms Mg²⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻, so two chlorides are needed per magnesium for zero total charge.

Writing a chemical formula requires correct element symbols, known oxidation/charge assumptions and smallest integer ratio. The school-level criss-cross technique can be a shortcut, but its output must be checked using a charge ledger.
Polyatomic ions, when taught, must be treated as intact groups in formula writing: Ca²⁺ with nitrate NO₃⁻ yields Ca(NO₃)₂. Parentheses matter because the 2 multiplies the entire nitrate group.
subtopics.representation: Show a charge-balance line: Mg²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻ → MgCl₂; the overall +2−2=0 appears below the ions.

worked_example.problem: Write the simplest neutral formula for Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
steps: Use cation Al³⁺ and anion O²⁻.
Find smallest equal positive/negative total: +6 and −6.
This takes two aluminium ions and three oxide ions.
The formula is Al₂O₃.
worked_example.check: The ion charge ledger gives 2(+3)+3(−2)=0; total positive and negative charges cancel exactly.

misconception.wrong: A subscript is the charge on a single ion.
misconception.why: Subscript is the number of each component, and is chosen to achieve total neutrality.
misconception.repair: Separate individual ion charge from total charge after multiplying by counts.

subtopics.title: Molecular and formula-unit masses
subtopics.entry_question: Why is a formula unit of CaCO₃ heavier than a water molecule even though neither formula is very long?
core1a_paragraphs: Relative atomic mass compares atomic masses against a reference scale. Molecular mass or formula-unit mass adds the appropriate atomic masses of all atoms in the specified unit, applying every subscript and parenthesis.
To calculate water's molecular mass, use 2×1+16 =18 in approximate atomic-mass units. Calcium carbonate's formula-unit mass uses Ca≈40, C≈12 and three O≈16 each: 40+12+48=100.
This unit is different from a single macroscopic gram. The corresponding molar mass has the same numerical value expressed in g/mol; understanding why requires the mole concept, addressed in C04.
subtopics.representation: Use a formula ledger table with element, atomic count, atomic-mass contribution and sum. Keep atom number separate from mass per atom.

subtopics.title: Chemical symbols and electron-dot introduction
subtopics.entry_question: What does a single dot around a chemical symbol stand for in an electron-dot diagram?
core1a_paragraphs: Chemical symbols identify elements. Electron-dot sketches focus on outer electrons in a chosen shell model, not the protons and neutrons of the atom. In a simple dot representation each dot denotes one valence electron, while a bond line conventionally denotes a shared pair.

For sodium (2,8,1), one dot near Na represents its one valence electron. Chlorine (2,8,7) can be represented with seven dots. The dot scheme is a transition from shell counting to chemical bonding, not a proof of a particular solid or reaction.

An ion's symbol carries a net charge. For Na⁺, the outer electron has been removed relative to the neutral atom; for Cl⁻ one has been added. Dot diagrams may depict this with brackets and charges, but a diagram must preserve the electron ledger.
subtopics.representation: Side-by-side write Na· and [Na]⁺, with 'one outer electron removed' label; write chlorine's seven dots and [Cl]⁻ after addition. Dot positions are schematic, not electron orbit locations.

worked_example.problem: Sketch valence dots for oxygen in a simple school model.
steps: O has atomic number 8, shell configuration 2,6.
The outermost shell contains six electrons.
Place six dots around the O symbol in a way that keeps the six-count visible.
Recognise this is an electron accounting representation, not exact spatial electron positions.
worked_example.check: The dot count equals six outer-shell electrons, not eight total electrons.

misconception.wrong: Each dot shows an atom's entire electron inventory.
misconception.why: The conventional Lewis-dot symbol typically shows valence electrons only.
misconception.repair: Distinguish full electron configuration from outer-shell dot count.

demands.worked_reasoning: O has 2,6, so six dots, not eight. Mg has 2,8,2, so two outer dots.

demands.title: Do dots prove a bond?
demands.core1a_explanation: The dot sketch represents possible outer electron bookkeeping. Formation and stability require additional chemical warrants.
demands.worked_reasoning: A hypothetical dot transfer might satisfy an octet but fail energetic or structural conditions.
demands.independent_check: State what the representation cannot prove.
hints: Identify the atoms, ions and system boundary.
State the composition, count or charge quantity that is conserved.
Translate the conservation rule into a diagram or equation without guessing the final outcome.

core1b.predict: Predict a result, and name the chemical law or model that could justify it.
core1b.attempt: A student argues 'My dot diagram gives both elements eight electrons, so the compound must exist.' Assess.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild from atom identities and conservation of mass/charge, explaining each representation step.
core1b.diagnose: Evaluate the tempting route: A correct dot count is experimental compound identification
core1b.repair: Require independent chemical evidence, charge and energetic considerations.
core1b.boundary: Can a crystal be chemically identified by its dot sketch alone?
core1b.model_response: Not established. Electron counting and octet compatibility are necessary checks for some simple models, not proof of thermodynamic stability or observed formation.

subtopics.source_notes: C03 introduction; detailed bonding taught in C07.
